newsitem.title: USA: US Commerce official sees trend growth in 3rd qtr.
newsitem.headline: US Commerce official sees trend growth in 3rd qtr.

text.p: A senior Commerce Department official Friday brushed aside worries that the economy may be slowing too abruptly.

"The economy is slowing down only in the sense that it has gotten out of the passing lane that it was in in the scond quarter and is learning to drive at the speed limit," said Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich.

He told Reuters Financial Television that he expects the economy to grow at "roughly around trend" in the third quarter after expanding by 4.7 percent in the second. Most economists put trend growth at just over two percent.
Ehrlich said corporate investment and inventory rebuilding should add to growth in the third quarter.
"We ought to see growth above two percent for the second half of the year," he said.
That means that growth for the year as a whole is likely to top the Clinton administration's 2.6 percent forecast, he added. "The risks to our forecast are all on the upside," Ehrlich said.
He declined comment on Federal Reserve policy, but noted that inflation has abated in the last several months.
The Commerce Department reported earlier that the U.S. trade deficit fell 6.6 percent to $10.83 billion in August. But that was still well above levels seen earlier in the year.
Ehrlich acknowledged that the strength of the dollar last year might be one of the factors behind the higher deficits, but he was unsure if it was the major one.

He said that exports were set to rise to record levels again this year, despite what he called "some adverse currency movements" and faster economic growth in the United States than elsewhere in the industrial world.

"The United States ... is now the growth locomotive of the industrialized world," Ehrlich said. "And yet our exports continue to grow faster than our imports. That speaks to the underlying competitiveness of the U.S. economy."
He said he expects growth overseas to pick up, helping to buttress U.S. exports.
"The European economy is growing slow," Ehrlich said. "We'd like it to grow faster."
He forecast a continued narrowing of the U.S. trade deficit with Japan as that country restructures its economy.
"We're going to continue to see improvement," Ehrlich said. "The Japanese economy is finally beginning to change in the important structural ways that it must."
The trade gap with Japan narrowed by 11.8 percent in August. By contrast, the deficit with China shot up by 23.4 percent, surpassing the gap with Japan.

Ehrlich said U.S. imports from China were boosted in August by shipments of Chinese-made toys, Christmas decorations and other seasonal items. "We'll see some falling back in the bilateral trade deficit with China in the months ahead," he said.
